title: Spotted Dick
subtitle: Steamed suet pudding with currants and lemon
excerpt: A British steamed suet sponge studded with currants and scented with lemon zest. Served warm with custard. Dense, comforting, and resolutely old-fashioned.

recipe.sourceNotes: Spotted Dick is one of the oldest surviving British puddings, first recorded in print in Alexis Soyer's 'The Modern Housewife or Menagere' (1849). The name is matter-of-fact: 'spotted' refers to the currants (which appear as spots in the cut pudding) and 'dick' is thought to be a corruption of 'dough' or 'dicked' (a dialect word for pressed or flattened). It was historically boiled in a cloth, then pudding basins became standard. The suet gives the sponge its characteristic dense, moist texture that is very different from a butter sponge.

recipeTools.notes: Large enough to hold the pudding basin with a lid for steaming.

content.text: The water in the steamer pan must not boil dry: check the level every 30 minutes and top up with boiling water as needed. The pudding is done when a skewer inserted into the centre comes out clean and the sponge has pulled away slightly from the sides of the basin. Serve warm with custard poured over.
Grease a 1 litre pudding basin well. Mix together the flour, suet, sugar, currants, and lemon zest in a bowl.
Beat together the milk and egg. Pour into the dry ingredients and mix to a soft, dropping consistency.
Spoon into the pudding basin. Cover tightly with a double layer of greased baking paper and a layer of foil, both pleated in the centre to allow the pudding to expand. Secure with string.

Set the basin in a large saucepan on a trivet or upturned saucer. Pour in boiling water to come halfway up the sides of the basin. Cover and steam over low heat for 1 hour 30 minutes. Top up the water every 30 minutes.
Remove the basin and leave to rest for 5 minutes. Run a knife around the edge and turn out onto a warm plate. Serve immediately with custard.
